# star-distance — concept pass (CREATIVE.md §1) — generated by episodes/star-distance/lines.py

**Governing image:** the parallax blink — one point that jumps against what lies behind it (thumb → near star → breathing star → galaxy).

**Motif:** the circle of the lens — the eye, the eyepiece, Leavitt’s loupe, the dome of Mount Wilson, Gaia’s shield.

| L | line | A literal · B metaphor · C transformation → pick |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | Hold up your thumb at arm's length, and look past it, at something far away. | A: a child at a window · B: a ruler held up to the sky · C: the viewer’s own thumb against the night — PICK C (the method in your own hand) |
| 1 | Now close one eye… then the other. Your thumb jumps. | A: two photographs side by side · B: a car passing trees · C: your own blink, thumb leaping — PICK C (governing image, born) |
| 2 | Nothing moved but your point of view. And that little jump, it turns out, can measure the distance to the stars. | A: a diagram of two eyes · B: a lighthouse beam · C: the nail itself becomes the Moon — PICK C (★ the thumb becomes the sky) |
| 3 | For thousands of years, people looked up at those lights and wondered how far away they were. | A: Stonehenge · B: a child asking · C: rise through the sky past the Moon — PICK C (one continuous rise) |
| 4 | But the stars never seemed to move. They looked pinned in place, like jewels in a cabinet. | A: a planetarium dome · B: a ceiling painted with stars · C: the sky becomes a collector’s case — PICK C (★ the “fixed stars” made literal) |
| 5 | Astronomers called them the fixed stars. And for two thousand years, nobody could say how far away a single one of them was. | A: a book of ancient astronomy · B: a blank ruler · C: the blank label under one pinned star — PICK C |
| 6 | The answer took a split telescope in Prussia, a woman with a magnifying glass, and one word scrawled on a glass plate. | A: three names written · B: three keys on a ring · C: three cards in the same cabinet — PICK C (real faces by 0:45) |
| 7 | And the answer turned out to be far stranger than the question. | A: a plain title · B: a door closing · C: the case gathers to a point and the title appears — PICK C |
| 8 | A star is a dot of light. It has no size you can see, no edge, no label. | A: a star close up (wrong: it would have a disc) · B: a full stop on a page · C: magnify and magnify, it stays a point — PICK C (true) |
| 9 | A bright star could be close… or huge, and very far away. From here, the two look exactly the same. | A: two stars labelled · B: car headlights · C: candle near, lighthouse far — PICK C (brightness lies) |
| 10 | To find the distance, you need something you can measure. And the first clue was the one in your own eyes. | A: an eye chart · B: binoculars · C: the dots become the light in your own eyes — PICK C |
| 11 | Clue one: the wobble. | A: a title card · B: a pendulum · C: the blink keeps the beat — PICK C |
| 12 | Your eyes see from two places, a few centimetres apart. So a near thing seems to jump against a far one. That jump is called parallax. | A: a textbook diagram · B: two torches · C: the sightlines drawn out of the real eyes past the real thumb — PICK C |
| 13 | Now spread your eyes as far apart as they could ever be: the two ends of the Earth's path around the Sun. | A: an orbit diagram · B: two lighthouses · C: your two eyes become the Earth’s two positions — PICK C (★ the body becomes the orbit) |
| 14 | Look at a nearby star in January, and again in July. Against the stars far behind it, it should shift, very slightly. | A: an animation of a star moving · B: two photos flicked · C: overlay the two fields like tracing paper — PICK C (★ the shift is found by overlaying) |
| 15 | Astronomers looked for that shift for centuries. So why did they see nothing? | A: a list of names · B: a fisherman with an empty net · C: three centuries of telescopes in a row, empty notebooks — PICK C |
| 16 | The shift was there. But for every star, it is less than one three-thousand-six-hundredth of a degree. | A: a number · B: a hair under a microscope · C: dive into a degree until one second is a hair — PICK C (★ a scale-dive into an angle) |
| 17 | In the 1830s, in Königsberg, Friedrich Bessel set out to catch it, with a telescope built for one job: measuring tiny angles. | A: Bessel’s portrait · B: a watchmaker’s bench · C: the angle’s sliver opens as the dome’s slit — PICK C |
| 18 | His heliometer cut the image of the sky in two, so he could slide one star onto another and read the gap between them. | A: a diagram of a split lens · B: two halves of a torn photo · C: the hand turns the screw and the halves slide — PICK C (how it works) |

| 20 | A fast crawl hinted that it was close. But how close? Night after night for more than a year, he measured it against two faint stars nearby. | A: a calendar · B: a candle burning down · C: the light of the nights sweeping round him — PICK C |
| 21 | In 1838 he had it: a shift of about a third of a second of arc. | A: Bessel smiling · B: a bell rung · C: the star moves and stops; a number — PICK C |
| 22 | That is the width of a small coin… seen from thirteen kilometres away. | A: a ruler · B: a hair from across a room · C: a coin on a far hill — PICK C (metaphor 1 of the ladder) |
| 23 | From that tiny angle, the rest is a triangle. Its base is the Earth's orbit, and its far point is the star. | A: trigonometry on a blackboard · B: a surveyor · C: the road becomes the triangle — PICK C |

| 28 | But there was a catch. Most stars are so far away that their wobble is far too small to measure. | A: an X over a triangle · B: a ruler that is too short · C: the page folds into a boat that sinks into the stars — PICK C (★ the method runs aground) |
